title: Pre-Wedding Photoshoot: Planning, Outfits, Poses and Costs — cv.cm
description: Plan a pre-wedding or engagement photoshoot: timeline, locations, 2–3 outfit changes, studio vs travel shoot, couple poses, contract questions and weather backup.
h1: How do you plan a pre-wedding photoshoot?
answer: Book the photographer or studio three to six months before the wedding, choose one or two locations that mean something to you, plan two or three outfit changes, and shoot in the last hours before sunset. Before you sign, confirm how many edited photos you get, whether RAW files are included, which outfits are in the package, and any extra fees.

body: A pre-wedding photoshoot is a portrait session of the couple, done weeks or months before the wedding. In China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Korea, Japan, Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and India it is a major part of wedding planning. The photos are often printed large for the wedding venue, made into an album, used on invitations, or shown as a slideshow at the reception. In many Western countries the same idea is called an engagement shoot, and it is usually shorter and more casual.

ul: Studio: indoor sets, rented gowns and suits, professional hair and makeup, many outfit changes in one day.
Local location: a park, old town, beach, campus or café near home, with your own clothes or rented outfits.
Travel shoot: a trip to a famous landscape or city with a photographer, sometimes in another country.

body: The session also works as a rehearsal. You get used to the photographer and to being in front of a camera, so you are more relaxed on the wedding day.

head: When
What to do
rows: Decide the style and budget; collect example photos you like; shortlist studios or photographers
Book and sign the contract; choose locations and season; apply for any location permits
Choose outfits and fittings; book hair and makeup; plan the shot list and props
Confirm the schedule, transport and a backup date; check sunrise and sunset times
Haircut or color, nails, try on everything with shoes; prepare the emergency kit
Eat, start hair and makeup early, arrive before the best light
Select photos, approve retouching, order the album and prints

body: If the photos are for the wedding venue or invitations, finish the shoot at least three months before the wedding. Album production and large prints can take several weeks.

For outdoor shoots, plan the main part for the last two hours before sunset. Look up the exact time for your date and place in your phone's weather app or an official calculator such as NOAA's Solar Calculator, because sunset time changes with the season and your latitude.

A place that means something to you usually gives better photos than a famous view: where you met, your first date, your school, a street you walk together, or a hobby place. Pick one or two locations close to each other so you do not lose the best light in traffic.

ul: Check rules before you go. Some parks, temples, museums and heritage sites need a permit for photo sessions, charge a fee, or ban tripods and drones.
Busy places: arrive early in the morning, do not block paths, and do not include strangers' faces without asking.
Each location should give at least two different backgrounds: open and wide, and close with texture (a wall, trees, a doorway).

body: Outfits: two or three changes is a good number for a half-day shoot. More changes means less time shooting.

ol: Formal: wedding gown and suit, or traditional wedding clothes such as a qipao, áo dài, hanbok, kimono, kebaya or lehenga.
Smart casual: a dress and shirt in matching colors, not identical prints.
Personal: clothes from your hobby, your uniforms, or the outfits from your first date.

body: Coordinate colors rather than matching them. Solid colors and soft patterns photograph better than logos, small stripes and neon colors. Bring comfortable shoes for walking between spots.
Props should tell your story: a bicycle, your pet, a book you both love, a picnic set, letters, an umbrella for rain, or balloons and a banner for a playful set. Use one or two props per setup.

body: A popular mix is a studio day for formal photos plus a short location session in your own clothes.

sections.h: Couple poses that work for anyone
body: Most couples are not models. Give them simple actions instead of fixed poses, and shoot in burst.

ul: Back hug: one partner stands behind and wraps the arms around the other's waist; both look at each other or at the camera.
Forehead kiss: shoot from the side, with the light coming from the side so both profiles are lit.
Walking hand in hand: walk slowly towards the camera, talk, look at each other. Then walk away and look back.
Looking at the view: stand together with hands joined and look at the landscape; place the couple about one third of the way into the scene.
Nose to nose: faces close, eyes closed, smiling. Good for shy couples.
Sitting together: on steps or a bench, one leaning on the other's shoulder.
Twirl: one partner spins the other under the arm; use burst.
Whisper: one whispers a joke or a secret into the other's ear for a real laugh.

body: Make sure hands are doing something: holding the other person's hand, resting on a waist or shoulder, or holding a prop. Loose hands hanging at the side look awkward. If one partner is camera-shy, start with shots from behind or with only hands, then move closer. The bridal poses guide on this shelf covers solo dress poses.
Two faces at different distances need more depth of field than a single portrait. If one face is sharp and the other is soft, close the aperture.

body: On a phone: use 1x for full-length shots and 2x for half-body. Tap the face of the partner nearest the camera to focus and set exposure. Portrait mode can blur one face if the two are far apart in depth; stand closer together or turn portrait mode off.
Packages that look cheap can become expensive through extras. Ask these questions before you pay a deposit, and get the answers in writing:

ol: How many edited (retouched) photos are included, and what does each extra photo cost?
Do we receive all the unedited files, or only the selected ones? Are RAW files included?
How many outfits are included? Are premium gowns or suits an extra charge?
Are hair and makeup included, and for how many looks?
How many hours and how many locations? Who pays location fees, entry tickets and permits?
Are transport, travel and the photographer's meals or hotel extra?
What does the album include: size, number of pages, frames, large prints?
When will we receive the photos? Is there a fee for faster delivery?
What happens if it rains: free rescheduling, an indoor backup, or a fee?
What are the deposit, cancellation and refund rules?
Can the studio use our photos in its advertising? Can we say no?

body.note: Ask to see a full set from one real couple, not only the best pictures from many couples. It shows what an ordinary session looks like.

body: Always have a backup date or an indoor location. Light rain or cloud can still work: clouds give soft light, and a clear umbrella makes a nice prop. Strong wind, heavy rain or extreme heat are reasons to move.

ul: Too many outfits: each change takes 30 to 60 minutes with hair and makeup. Two or three are enough.
Shooting at noon: hard shadows and squinting. Move into shade or wait for the late afternoon.
No food or water: tired couples stop smiling. Bring snacks and water with a straw.
New shoes: break them in before the day.
No time for travel: allow time to move between locations and change clothes before sunset.
Forgetting the files: back up the delivered photos in two places, and remove GPS location before posting if you shot near your home.

faq.q: How long before the wedding should we do pre-wedding photos?
faq.a: Three to six months before is common. That leaves time for retouching, an album and prints if the photos will be shown at the wedding or used on invitations.

faq.q: How many outfits should we bring to a pre-wedding shoot?
faq.a: Two or three for a half-day shoot: one formal, one smart casual and one personal. Each change takes time for clothes, hair and makeup.

faq.q: What is the difference between a pre-wedding shoot and an engagement shoot?
faq.a: They are similar. A pre-wedding shoot in Asia is often a full production with wedding gowns and studio sets, while an engagement shoot is usually shorter and more casual.

faq.q: What should we not wear for pre-wedding photos?
faq.a: Avoid large logos, thin stripes, neon colors and identical outfits. Coordinate colors instead, and choose clothes and shoes you can move and sit in comfortably.

faq.q: What if it rains on our pre-wedding shoot day?
faq.a: Agree on a backup date or an indoor location in the contract. Light rain can work with clear umbrellas, but heavy rain or strong wind is a reason to reschedule.
